newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk banks widen short FX positions, reserves jump.
newsitem.headline: Turk banks widen short FX positions, reserves jump.

text.p: Turkish banks have widened their short foreign exchange positions and the central bank has boosted its reserves as a new secularist government has eased months of political uncertainty, bankers say.

Central bank reserves have climbed by about $1.6 billion since June 20 when President Suleyman Demirel asked secularist Mesut Yilmaz to form a new government. The previous Islamist-led coalition of Necmettin Erbakan collapsed under pressure from the military after months of bitter conflict with the secularist establishment.
According to central bank figures obtained by Reuters, the central bank's foreign exchange reserves stood at $16.8 billion on Tuesday, up sharply from $15.2 billion on June 20.
Parliament is to hold a confidence vote in Yilmaz's government on Saturday, which the coalition is widely expected to win.
Bankers say the change of government and early action by the new left-right coalition has allowed banks to widen their short foreign exchange positions and invest in Turkish lira instruments.
"The central bank is now the best buyer in the foreign exchange market. Banks may continue to fund themselves through open foreign exchange positions," said one banker.

Economic as well as political uncertainties have eased. On Monday Gunes Taner, state minister for the treasury, said the new government would not go for a one-off devaluation or intervene in interest rates.

The government gave the first signal of a new borrowing policy last week when it met almost all of total bids worth 290.3 trillion at an auction of nine-month T-bills. The cost was a rise in the maximum yield to 124.47 percent.
The Treasury sold 229.1 trillion lira of 308-day bills at a maximum yield of 125.08 percent on Tuesday.
The former government stopped T-bill auctions to sell inflation-indexed two-year bonds which made up 15 percent of the total debt of 4,027 trillion lira ($26.8 billion).
Bankers say the new government was expected to continue zero-coupon Treasury auctions regularly and determine interest rates in line with market conditions.
They say banks have widened their foreign exchange positions to benefit from the high margin between the lira depreciation rate and relatively higher domestic interest rates.
Turkey has been keeping the lira depreciation rate on a par with inflation, which economists expect to be at around 75 to 80 percent this year.

"The central bank now acts as the major foreign currency buyer in the market where most of the banks tended to hold lira instruments. The lira could have been stronger if the central bank did not buy," a bank official said.

Bankers say the central bank foreign currency purchases also help banks fund themselves in the market, tightened by the high volume Treasury borrowings, which drained a net 265 trillion lira in the past two weeks out of nominal T-bill sales of about 520 trillion lira.

The Treasury uses the proceeds of the auctions to repay its debt to the central bank -- a move which will improve the central bank balance sheet and enable the bank to narrow its reserve money and increase control over the money market.
